```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Microsoft Fabric brings SQL warehouses, lakehouses and other analytics
services into one platform. Use Fabric data in a Shiny app with each visitor's Microsoft account.
For a Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL endpoint, or SQL Database, query with DBI
or dbplyr. For other Fabric work, call fabricQueryR functions with the same
sign-in.

## Try the guided demo

Run `shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("fabric")` in your R console.
The guide asks for the SQL `server`, `database`, Entra `tenant_id` and
`client_id`, then whether your registration is public PKCE or confidential.
It shows where to find each value, registration instructions and your local
callback. You can pause until an administrator grants access.

Install `fabricQueryR`, `odbc`, `processx` and, for masked secrets, `askpass`;
install Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 on your computer too. The app opens locally
and runs its identity query only when you click **Run example query**.
For scripted setup, pass those names as arguments; `driver` can override
the installed driver's name. See [Guided cloud demos](cloud-demos.html).

If you have no workspace, check [Fabric trial eligibility](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/get-started/fabric-trial).
You still need an Entra app registration and permission to use a SQL item.

## Set up SQL access

In R, run `install.packages(c("fabricQueryR", "odbc"))`. Install
[Microsoft ODBC Driver 18](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/odbc/download-odbc-driver-for-sql-server)
for your operating system too. Copy the server and database from the item's SQL connection settings.
Users need access to that item and its data; see
[Fabric SQL connectivity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/data-warehouse/connectivity).

Create an Entra Web app registration with permission to access SQL on a
user's behalf. Register `http://localhost:8100` as its redirect URI.
Save these values in a local `.Renviron` file and restart R:

```text
OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID=your-tenant-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
```

Use the [Microsoft registration steps](oauth-setup.html#register-a-microsoft-entra-app).
For this first SQL app, add **Azure SQL Database** delegated
`user_impersonation`. Fabric API permissions are needed only when adding
the API examples later in this guide.

| Value | Where to find it |
| --- | --- |
| `server` | Open the Warehouse or Lakehouse **SQL analytics endpoint**, then copy its **SQL connection string** server |
| `database` | The database/catalog shown in those connection settings |
| Tenant ID, client ID, secret | Your [Entra app registration](oauth-setup.html#register-a-microsoft-entra-app) |

Copy the server hostname, without a connection-string prefix or credentials.
Share the item with the app's users and grant access to its data. A workspace
or item ID from the browser URL isn't the SQL server hostname.

## A complete app

Save this as `example.R`, replacing the server and database:

```{r app}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

client <- oauth_db_microsoft_client(
  services = "sql",
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_fabric_sql(
    auth$connection,
    server = "example.datawarehouse.fabric.microsoft.com",
    database = "Reporting"
  )

  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT CURRENT_USER AS database_user")
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)
```

Run `source("example.R")` and open
`http://localhost:8100`. Sign in to run the query; signing out clears the
output.

The query shows the database user. Replace it with SQL for your tables.
Call `con()` inside the reactive expression to get the DBI connection;
you can also use it with dbplyr.

## List workspaces

To list the workspaces a user can access, change the client's services to
`services = c("sql", "fabric")`. The Fabric preset requests and requires
the delegated `Workspace.Read.All` and `Item.Read.All` permissions. Add both
to the Entra registration alongside SQL access, even if this example only
lists workspaces.

Add `verbatimTextOutput("workspaces")` to the UI and put this inside
`server()`:

```{r workspaces}
fabric <- oauth_db_fabric_api(auth$connection)

output$workspaces <- renderPrint({
  fabric$call(fabricQueryR::fabric_workspaces)
})
```

Pass a fabricQueryR function and its arguments to `$call()`. The client
supplies the user's credentials and returns the function's result.

## Choose additional services

Include the services your app uses in `oauth_db_microsoft_client()` and
configure their delegated permissions in the Entra registration:

| `services` entry | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `"sql"` | Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL endpoint, and SQL Database |
| `"fabric"` | Workspace and item discovery |
| `"onelake"` | OneLake files and tables |
| `"dax"` | Semantic model queries |
| `"kql"` | KQL queries |
| `"graphql"` | GraphQL queries |

Users need access to each workspace and item they query. SQL, OneLake,
and semantic models have their own permissions.

For KQL, include `"kql"` in the client's services. With `fabric` created
as above, replace the table output with:

```{r kql}
output$rows <- renderTable({
  fabric$call(
    fabricQueryR::fabric_kql_query,
    cluster = "https://example.kusto.fabric.microsoft.com",
    database = "Events",
    query = "Events | take 20"
  )
})
```

## Read a Lakehouse table

Use `services = c("fabric", "onelake")` to discover a Lakehouse and read its
tables. Add these services to the client if you're also using SQL.

`fabric_item()` returns a fabricQueryR object with methods such as
`$read_table()`. Put the lookup inside `reactive()` so it runs again if
the signed-in account changes:

```{r lakehouse}
lakehouse <- reactive({
  fabric$call(
    fabricQueryR::fabric_item,
    workspace = "workspace-guid",
    item = "lakehouse-guid"
  )
})

output$rows <- renderTable({
  lakehouse()$read_table("Orders", limit = 100L)
})
```

Warehouse objects offer `$sql_query(sql)`, and semantic model objects offer
`$dax_query(dax)`. Include `"sql"` or `"dax"` in the client's services
for those methods. See fabricQueryR's help for their arguments.

## Connection options

The SQL helper uses ODBC by default. For ADBC, install fabricQueryR's ADBC
dependencies and the MSSQL driver, then pass `backend = "adbc"` to
`oauth_db_fabric_sql()`. Options such as `timeout` and `read_only` go to
`fabricQueryR::fabric_sql_connect()`.

The helper manages its own DBI connection. Your app must close connections
it opens through fabricQueryR functions or resource methods.

## Use an existing sign-in

If your shinyOAuth client uses different token target names, map the
services to those targets:

```{r targets}
fabric <- oauth_db_fabric_api(
  auth$connection,
  targets = c(fabric = "discovery", sql = "reporting", onelake = "files")
)
```

The mapping replaces the defaults. For one service without a named target,
use `targets = list(kql = NULL)`. DAX and GraphQL share the Power BI
resource and must use the same target; different resources need different
targets.

To call a fabricQueryR function directly, pass
`token = fabric$token_provider()`. `?oauth_db_fabric` shows the alternative
for a single service.

See [Authentication and sessions](authorization.html) for target settings
and saved query results.
